data.cultural_impact: The name Prophet Jonah holds immense significance in Christianity, where he is remembered as a prophet who was swallowed by a whale and then spat back out after he repented his sins. In Islamic tradition, this prophet is also known as Younus. In both traditions, Younus is a symbol of forgiveness, and his story serves as a reminder of God's mercy and compassion towards sinners.
data.spiritual_significance: In Islamic tradition, Prophet Younus is considered a prophet who was chosen by God to carry out a specific mission. His story teaches valuable lessons, such as the importance of obeying God's commands and the consequences of disobedience. spiritually, his name signifies God's endless mercy and compassion towards sinners who repent and turn back to Him. Through the story of Younus, Muslims can learn to seek forgiveness from God and strive to live a life that is pleasing to Him.

historical_references.reference: Prophet Yunus (Jonah) in the Quran, who was ordered by Allah to deliver a warning to the people of Nineveh. When they ignored the warning and continued in their disobedience, Prophet Yunus asked Allah to save him from them and was swallowed by a whale (as a test of faith). After repenting and praying, he was released and the people of Nineveh were saved from destruction when they repented.
historical_references.time_period: Approximately 6th Century BCE (mentioned in the Quran, around 7th Century CE)
historical_references.context: An Old Testament prophet and a major prophet in Islam.

historical_references.reference: The story of Prophet Yunus is also found in the Bible, where he is called Jonah. He was a Hebrew prophet who was sent by God to the city of Nineveh to warn the inhabitants to repent of their sins. When they refused to listen, Jonah boarded a ship to Tarshish in an attempt to escape God's command. However, the ship was thrown into turmoil by a great storm, and the crew blamed Jonah for the misfortune. They threw him overboard, but he was swallowed by a whale and remained inside for three days and three nights. Eventually, he was thrown up onto the shore, and God instructed him to return to Nineveh and deliver the warning again. This time, the people repented and were spared from destruction.
historical_references.time_period: Approximately 8th Century BCE (mentioned in the Bible, around 4th Century BCE)
historical_references.context: An Old Testament prophet and a major figure in Judeo-Christian tradition.
